extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy and aesthetics (general educated audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical account of genius, æsthetic contemplation, the nature of beauty and the sublime, and how art communicates Platonic Ideas by freeing knowledge from the service of the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of imagination as necessary condition of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary strength of imagination accompanies, and is indeed a necessary condition of genius; imagination extends the intellectual horizon of the man of genius beyond the objects which actually present themselves to him, enabling him to construct the whole out of the little that comes into his actual apperception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination allows the genius to see in things not what Nature has actually made but what she endeavoured to make; however, imagination alone is not sufficient for genius—many with much imagination are mere dreamers who use fantasy to gratify ego and produce ordinary novels that merely entertain. The text contrasts the productive, Idea-seeing imagination of genius with fanciful daydreaming that fixes on relations congenial to the individual's humour (anti-pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of Ideas (knowledge independent of the principle of sufficient reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius consists in the capacity for knowing, independently of the principle of sufficient reason, not individual things (which exist only in their relations) but the Ideas of such things; the genius grasps the enduring form or Idea rather than contingent relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This non-causal, non-relational mode of knowledge is the basis of æsthetic insight and is opposed to the ordinary, relation-seeking cognition that serves the will and science. The work of art communicates this Idea to others by reproducing it removed from accidental relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's technical role: abstracting the Idea from the actual
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist, who knew only the Idea and not the actual, reproduces in his work the pure Idea, abstracting it from the actual and omitting all disturbing accidents; the work of art thus facilitates the knowledge of the Idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possessing the eyes to see the Idea is inborn (genius), but enabling others to see it (the technical side of art) is acquired skill. Good art lets the spectator 'see the world through the artist's eyes' and so more readily elicits æsthetic pleasure than direct contemplation of nature often does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predominance of knowledge over will (pure knowing) as the mark of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression of genius in a face consists in a decided predominance of knowledge over will, and consequently a knowledge that is entirely devoid of relation to will (i.e., pure knowing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This manifests outwardly in a keen, steady glance bearing the stamp of perception and contemplation, contrasted with ordinary countenances where will predominates and knowledge serves merely as a lamp to light practical ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aversion to mathematics and practical prudence as a corollary of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The disinclination of men of genius to direct their attention to the content of the principle of sufficient reason first shows itself, with regard to the ground of being, as dislike of mathematics; the logical, memory-dependent method of mathematics is antagonistic to genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical anecdotes (Alfieri, Goethe) are cited as examples; conversely, admirable mathematicians often lack susceptibility to fine art. Prudence (capacity for quick comprehension of causal relations) and genius tend not to co-exist while each is operative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of genius to verge on madness
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius and madness touch and even pass into each other: poetical inspiration has been called a kind of madness; persons of genius are often subject to violent emotions and irrational passions and may exhibit weaknesses akin to madness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation ties this to the same intellectual disposition: both madmen and geniuses have correct perception of the immediate present but err concerning absent relations—madmen by broken continuity of memory filling gaps with fictions; geniuses by neglecting causal/relational knowledge in order to apprehend Ideas, which leads to extremes, inability to 'hit the mean', and occasional irrational action. Examples: Ajax, King Lear, Ophelia; biographies of Rousseau, Byron, Alfieri.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic pleasure's two inseparable constituents: Idea and will-less subject
rubrics_metrics.description: In the æsthetical mode of contemplation there are two inseparable constituent parts—the knowledge of the object not as individual thing but as Platonic Idea, and the self-consciousness of the knowing person not as individual but as pure will-less subject of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both arise when one abandons the principle of sufficient reason and is delivered from the service of the will. The pleasure experienced stems from this duality; sometimes one constituent predominates over the other depending on the object of contemplation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as fitness: objects that readily represent their Ideas excite the sense of the beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty (in the objective sense) consists in the fittingness of natural forms such that the Ideas individualized in them readily present themselves to us; natural beauty particularly invites æsthetic observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When objects by their manifold yet definite and distinct form easily become representatives of their Ideas, they facilitate the transition to pure perception and so produce æsthetic satisfaction. The vegetable world and simple country scenes are given as especially apt examples; if objects do not readily present the Idea, they fail to elicit this pleasure (anti-pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime grounded in modification of will-less perception (subjective side)
rubrics_metrics.description: The impression of the sublime depends altogether upon a modification of the subjective side of æsthetic pleasure—that is, upon the state in which knowledge is freed from the service of the will and the subject becomes a pure will-less knower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text announces an extended treatment later, but here states that the sublime arises from this altered subjective disposition rather than from objective 'fittingness' alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light and transparent colours produce æsthetic delight by enabling pure perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Light is the pleasantest and most gladdening of things because it is the correlative and condition of the most perfect kind of perceptive knowledge—the only knowledge which does not affect the will; transparent colours directly excite keen delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why reflections in water and play of light are aesthetically moving: they present the completest and purest perceptions. By contrast, senses more directly tied to the will (taste, smell, touch) are 'ignobler' and give pleasures/displeasures connected to willing.
